overview: Yayoi is an archaeological period, not one kingdom or a single people. The atlas shows it twice: a western Japanese shape from 400 to 323 BCE and a larger shape from 100 to 200 CE, leaving a 423-year map gap inside a history that continued. Long chronologies place wet-field rice farming in northern Kyushu by about the tenth or ninth century BCE, but adoption moved unevenly; Jomon-derived, post-Jomon, shell-midden, farming, fishing, and mixed communities coexisted across the archipelago. Villages raised rice, hunted, fished, stored grain, made pottery and textiles, and exchanged stone and metal goods. Some settlements gained moats, defended enclosures, rich burials, specialist workshops, and leaders, yet regional paths differed. Chinese court histories later describe many Wa communities, envoys, warfare, and Himiko; they are outsider texts about particular polities, not a census of every Yayoi household. Archaeology adds houses, fields, bones, jars, tools, and food remains while leaving many voices unheard. Around the mid-third century, keyhole tombs and new political networks mark the Kofun transition. Neither atlas endpoint is a founding, collapse, or disappearance.

periods.title: About 900 to 600 BCE: paddies begin in northern Kyushu
periods.summary: Accelerator mass spectrometry moved the beginning of wet-field rice cultivation in northern Kyushu back toward the tenth century BCE. Early farmers still depended heavily on stone tools, and the longer chronology means change was slower than older textbook stories suggested.

periods.title: 600 to 400 BCE: farming settlements develop unevenly
periods.summary: On the Fukuoka plain, settlements such as Itazuke combined moats, storage pits, engineered field ridges, and water channels. Korean Peninsula influences joined older local practices, so the transition was layered rather than a clean replacement of one lifeway everywhere at once.

periods.title: 400 to 323 BCE: the first atlas window
periods.summary: The earlier atlas feature covers western Honshu, Shikoku, and much of Kyushu in a three-part polygon. Its border is a modern display device, not a fourth-century kingdom, and it vanishes at 323 BCE while Yayoi archaeology continues, not a historical boundary.

periods.title: 323 to 100 BCE: settlements grow during the map gap
periods.summary: At Yoshinogari, sporadic early villages developed into a moated settlement, and middle-period construction added a large outer moat, leader burials, and extensive jar cemeteries. One site illustrates social change but cannot stand for the whole archipelago or its entire period.

periods.title: 100 to 1 BCE: bronze ritual and regional power
periods.summary: Ritual bronze bells changed in size, decoration, and likely use while farming societies developed in different ways. Their distributions and imagery illuminate regional ceremonies; they do not identify one Yayoi religion, capital, or political ruler for the whole archipelago uniformly.

periods.title: 1 BCE to 57 CE: northern Kyushu faces Han
periods.summary: By 57 CE, an envoy from the polity called Na in Chinese records reached the Later Han court. The inscribed gold seal associated with that grant belongs to diplomatic hierarchy, not proof that people across the archipelago read Chinese locally.

periods.title: 57 to 100 CE: the seal outlives its embassy
periods.summary: The five-character gold seal was reportedly unearthed on Shikanoshima in 1784 and is linked by Fukuoka City Museum to the Later Han account. Its survival connects text, artifact, and place, while the exact path into the ground remains unknown today.

periods.title: 100 to 180 CE: the second atlas window expands east
periods.summary: The later atlas polygon retains all twelve tested western members of the earlier shape and adds tested points in central and northeastern Honshu. Expansion in this display echoes regional spread only loosely; it is not a surveyed border or unified state.

periods.title: 180 to 238 CE: conflict and Himiko enter written history
periods.summary: The Wei history, compiled around 297, retrospectively describes disturbances among Wa communities followed by agreement on the woman ruler Himiko. This is invaluable outsider testimony, but its geography, terminology, and courtly viewpoint require careful comparison with archaeology rather than literally.

periods.title: 238 to 300 CE: embassies, mirrors, and Kofun transition
periods.summary: Himiko sent an envoy to Wei in 238 or 239 and received prestigious gifts, including a recorded hundred mirrors. During the same broad century, new political networks and monumental tomb building developed; the Yayoi-to-Kofun change retained important continuities across regions.

sections.title: First, read the two atlas shapes carefully

items.text: The live index contains two exact records named “Yayoi”: `yayoi`, dated about 400 to 323 BCE, and `yayoi-100`, dated about 100 to 200 CE. They share the same imported summary and source lead, yet neither has a card or reviewed identity. The data therefore invite one explanation, not two invented civilizations.

The first feature is one MultiPolygon with three components, three rings, and 142 coordinate positions. Its tested members run from northern Kyushu through western Honshu and Shikoku; tested Tokyo, Nagoya, Kanazawa, Sendai, and Morioka remain outside. This is a dataset footprint, not an excavated frontier.

The second feature is also a three-component MultiPolygon, now with 246 positions. It contains every tested member of the early shape and adds tested Nagoya, Kanazawa, Tokyo, Chiba, Sendai, and Morioka. The later polygon visualizes expansion eastward but still simplifies sharply varied regional chronologies.

At 400 BCE, the raw world layer also assigns every tested Yayoi point to distant Magadha and Saharan pastoral polygons. Those impossible co-owners expose global ring or winding artifacts in the imported geometry. They are overlap warnings, not evidence that Indian or Saharan states governed ancient Japan.

The earlier id disappears at 323 BCE; the later one appears only at 100 CE and disappears at 200. Because the names and source summaries match and the tested early footprint nests inside the later one, one shared historical card is warranted. Distinct overrides preserve both dates and shapes rather than pretending one continuous border.

sections.title: A long period with many regional clocks

items.text: Rekihaku’s radiocarbon program places the beginning of northern Kyushu paddy cultivation around the tenth century BCE, roughly five centuries earlier than older chronologies. It also notes that iron arrived much later than rice. Early Yayoi should therefore not be reduced to a sudden “rice plus iron” package.

The longer chronology does not create more excavated houses or tombs. Researchers must ask whether early settlements were sparse, remains were concentrated in shorter episodes, or preservation misleads us. A twelve-hundred-year label is a framework built from changing pottery and dates, not a diary with every year filled.

Radiocarbon tests of skeletons long grouped as “Kanto Yayoi” found some belonged instead to Jomon or Kofun contexts, while others were securely Yayoi. Museum labels and skeletal shape alone can blur time. The correction shows why eastern expansion must be reconstructed specimen by specimen and site by site.

Early Fukuoka settlements preserved Korean Peninsula influences in pottery, houses, farming technology, and exchange, alongside strong continuities from earlier local traditions. “Yayoi” describes these layered archaeological patterns. It should not become a simple story in which one uniform incoming population instantly replaces everyone already living in the archipelago.

Hakata Bay sand-dune sites remind us that rice fields were never the only livelihood. Some communities occupied coastal settings better suited to fishing, salt production, and exchange. Hooks, net weights, scorched salt-making pottery, and graves reveal maritime work beside the better-known agricultural settlements of the nearby plains.

sections.title: Fields, food, storage, and busy hands

items.text: Itazuke combined a moated settlement on slightly raised ground with paddies, irrigation channels, and weirs below. Carbonized rice survives there. These finds show engineered water and crop systems in northern Kyushu; they do not mean the same schedule, field design, or diet existed in every region called Yayoi.

Yayoi jars came in different sizes and are interpreted partly as storage vessels for unhusked rice. At Itazuke, many storage pits lay inside the moat. As jars grew more common and shallow bowls declined, pottery proportions record changing food storage and preparation, though a vessel shape cannot identify its individual maker.

Yoshinogari’s official guide lists rice together with wheat, millet, beans, gourds, acorns, walnuts, wild mammals, birds, fish, sharks, and shellfish. The menu is a regional reconstruction, not a universal shopping list, but it firmly replaces the cartoon of everyone eating plain rice three times daily.

Coastal archaeology adds work often lost in inland farming stories. Stone hooks and net weights document fishing, while heat-damaged pottery may relate to salt making. Marine settlements also occupied exchange routes. A Yayoi meal and workday could smell of sea spray as readily as wet paddy mud.

Raised storehouses near Yoshinogari’s entrance are interpreted as places for ears of rice meant for food. Elevating stores helped organize and protect valuable harvests, but archaeology cannot tell us who received each bowl. Granaries reveal management and preservation; they do not by themselves prove a centralized tax system.

sections.title: Homes, work groups, clothing, and craft

items.text: The area interpreted as Yoshinogari’s public residential quarter has both pit dwellings and raised-floor structures; twenty-seven buildings are modern reconstructions based on archaeological plans. The postholes are evidence, while roofs, wall heights, and room activities require comparison and inference. Visitors see a tested model, not frozen ancient architecture.

Inside the defended southern enclosure, pit dwellings, high-floored buildings, watchtowers, and iron objects are interpreted as an elite residential zone. The contrast with other living areas supports social difference at this site. It should not be projected onto every Yayoi village or treated as a royal palace blueprint.

A northern Kyushu settlement study identifies recurring basic units of about five houses sharing storage facilities and a burial ground. Such units linked cooperation between settlements while also structuring tensions within them. They are archaeological household models, not a guarantee that every co-resident was biologically related.

The Wei history describes distinctive clothing for men and women and reports differences of status. It is a Chinese court text compiled around 297 CE, observing selected Wa communities through translators and envoys. Its clothing picture is valuable but cannot dress every region, century, child, or occupation in one costume.

Continental connections brought bronze and ironworking techniques as well as wet-rice cultivation to Kyushu. Metal did not instantly replace stone, and imported knowledge still required local skill: obtaining material, preparing molds, heating, casting, forging, repairing, and teaching. Finished artifacts preserve achievement more readily than the voices of craftspeople.

House clusters with shared storage and burial grounds are better evidence for everyday social units than a single monumental building. They suggest people coordinated food, space, and remembrance over time. The model does not reveal whether a household followed one marriage rule or whether servants, adoptees, and visitors also belonged.

The same household study treats storage and burial as communal institutions connecting small residential units to wider settlements. That makes family life political in a modest sense: cooperation over grain, work, and graves helped create communities. It does not establish that all authority descended automatically through fathers or mothers.

At Takuta-Nishibun in Saga, researchers are comparing people placed in jar coffins with people placed in pit graves using archaeological context and genomes. Two burial forms need not equal two peoples or ranks. The project models a careful question: test relationships instead of guessing family identity from containers.

A later dental study cites one published Yayoi child sample with deciduous-tooth caries, but the original report did not document whether those children came from farming or foraging settings. Childhood health can sometimes reach us through teeth; family teaching, play, affection, and daily chores remain far less visible.

Ancient genomes from northwestern Kyushu show diversity and gradual admixture rather than a single mass arrival at the period’s opening. Researchers explicitly tested whether sampled individuals were close relatives. Four skeletons cannot describe every family, but they warn against imagining a biologically uniform “Yayoi people.”

sections.title: Moats, leaders, conflict, and named polities

items.text: Yoshinogari changed from scattered villages to a moated community with leader mounds, jar cemeteries, stronger defenses, and large late buildings. The sequence documents concentrated power at one northern Kyushu site. Calling every Yayoi settlement a fortified capital would turn an exceptional archaeological record into a misleading template.

A large study counted traumatic injuries in skeletal samples and found higher frequencies in Yayoi than Jomon data, with middle-period clustering in northern Kyushu and Kinki. Its statistical model links local population pressure with violence. Correlation is not a confession: it cannot name attackers, motives, or every peaceful settlement.

Defenses and high-floor residences in Yoshinogari’s southern enclosure are interpreted as the setting of successive rulers and other village leaders. The evidence supports rank and guarded space, not a nationwide dynasty. Iron goods there mark privileged access while ordinary residents occupied different parts of the settlement.

The Wei history says more than one hundred Wa communities had existed and that about thirty maintained contact through envoys and scribes in its own day. It later describes agreement on Himiko after warfare. These are plural polities viewed from China, not a single state named “Yayoi.”

Kyushu National Museum dates Himiko’s embassy to 239 CE and records the Wei emperor’s gift of one hundred mirrors. Political gifts could materialize relationships between courts, but identifying excavated mirrors as her exact gifts remains debated. The exhibition’s story is a research interpretation, not a serial-number match.

The gold seal was reportedly found on Shikanoshima in 1784. Its five characters correspond to a Later Han account of a 57 CE grant to a ruler of Na in Wa. Artifact and text illuminate diplomacy across the sea, while neither tells us the full territory or population of Nakoku.

Dotaku bronze bells changed from functional-sounding forms toward larger ritual objects, some decorated with scenes of farming and animals. Casting thin bronze bodies demanded technical control. Their deliberate burial and varied regional patterns remain interpretive puzzles; an impressive bell is not a written constitution.

Rice, bronze, and iron technologies traveled through continuing exchange with continental Asia. Calling them “imports” should not erase the work of people in the archipelago who adapted crops, tools, and techniques to local soils and communities. Transmission is an achievement of learners and makers as well as travelers.

Modern AMS dating of around sixteen hundred items transformed the period’s chronology and made regional comparisons with Korea and China more precise. This discovery did not uncover a new king; it changed the calendar beneath familiar artifacts. Scientific measurement can rewrite a historical story without adding a single dramatic treasure.

Radiocarbon dating also corrected mixed skeletal collections in Kanto, moving some specimens into Jomon or Kofun time while retaining others as Yayoi. That is an archaeological achievement worth celebrating: admitting a label was too broad produces a truer past than protecting an elegant but inaccurate sequence.

sections.title: Learning, language, and one tiny written object

items.text: Archaeologists reconstructed Yoshinogari buildings by comparing excavated post patterns with structures across Japan, Korea, and China. The method teaches an important distinction: evidence anchors a model, but comparison fills gaps. No excavated classroom or curriculum lets us describe formal education for ordinary Yayoi children.

The Wei account mentions Wa envoys and scribes communicating with Chinese authorities. That proves specialized diplomatic literacy somewhere in the network described by the text, not universal reading. Farming, pottery, weaving, navigation, and ritual skills were likely learned socially, but the surviving sources do not preserve lesson plans.

Written sample: `漢委奴國王`. The conventional Japanese reading is “Kan no Wa no Na no Kokuō”; a close English rendering is “King of Na of Wa under Han.” These five Chinese seal-script characters form an official title, not a sentence in a Japanese alphabet.

Fukuoka City Museum links the seal to the Later Han record that an emperor granted a seal and cord in 57 CE to an envoy from Nakoku in Wa. Reportedly found at Shikanoshima in 1784, it is a Chinese imperial object connected with northern Kyushu diplomacy.

The seal is securely dated by its diplomatic context, but its discovery came about seventeen centuries later and the museum says it is “considered” the recorded seal. It demonstrates elite contact with Chinese writing. It does not demonstrate a local Japanese script, mass literacy, or children practicing characters at home.

sections.title: Medicine, teeth, water, sanitation, and toilets

items.text: Northern Kyushu farming samples had more carious teeth than a comparison group of Okinawan hunter-gatherers, and older agriculturalists showed more missing teeth and root caries associated with periodontal disease. Teeth record pain and diet-related risk. They do not reveal the names, remedies, or skill of healers.

The dental comparison separates regions and subsistence patterns instead of calling one group healthier in every respect. Its authors infer agricultural connections but work from selected skeletal collections. Food texture, carbohydrates, age, preservation, and sampling all matter; a cavity is evidence, not a complete medical chart.

The published child comparison reports low caries frequencies in one Yayoi deciduous-tooth sample, then immediately warns that its archaeological environment was not documented. This is useful restraint. We have no securely sourced pediatric manual, named doctor, vaccination, or hospital for the period, despite a park’s modern shorthand.

At Yoshinogari, springs provided water, and one well belongs to the late Yayoi through early Kofun transition. The official guide distinguishes discovered features from hoped-for future finds. Water access mattered for drinking and work, but a spring or well alone does not prove household pipes or systematic sewage treatment.

No restroom remains have been identified at Yoshinogari. The park cautiously compares human parasites found in moats at other sites and suggests waste may have entered ditches. That is not a discovered toilet, and certainly not deluxe plumbing. The honest answer is: people excreted; this dossier cannot draw their bathroom floor plan.

sections.title: Endings, continuities, and the road to Kofun

items.text: The Wei history reports Himiko’s rule, attendants, a communicating male intermediary, and later political turmoil around succession. It is a Chinese narrative shaped by court categories and translation. Even if its core events are accepted, Himiko’s death was not the end of all Yayoi communities or material traditions.

The 239 embassy and mirror grant belong near the end of many Yayoi chronologies. Kyushu National Museum connects prestigious mirrors with emerging political authority, while acknowledging interpretation through an exhibition story. Diplomacy helped new networks grow; it did not press a single instant “Kofun starts now” button.

Research on Kinki metal production stresses continuity across the Yayoi-to-Kofun transition even as large mounded tombs appeared. Bronze and iron manufacturing systems changed within local societies. Period names help organize evidence, but families, crafts, exchange routes, and fields did not vanish when archaeologists change the label.

Yoshinogari became largely deserted from the late third into early fourth century, while a smaller nearby settlement may have remained. The park links this shift to a society in which individuals held greater wealth and power. It is one site’s transformation, not proof of archipelago-wide abandonment.

Keyhole-shaped and other great mounds characterize Kofun political display from the third century onward. The atlas, however, drops `yayoi-100` at 200, before this broad transition is complete. The missing 323 BCE to 100 CE interval and early 200 endpoint are editorial seams, never cultural extinctions.

ending.text: By about 300 CE, keyhole tombs, changing metal-production networks, and new concentrations of authority mark the Kofun transition. This was neither the fall of a Yayoi kingdom nor the disappearance of its communities. Regional lifeways, farming, crafts, and exchange continued through a change in archaeological labels and political forms.
